Stated Claim / Post Context:
Key moments from UNGA Day 2: Speeches from Rodríguez, Zelensky, Pezeshkian | CNN

At the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Iran’s president struck a defiant tone while Ukraine’s Zelensky warned of the danger posed by Russia’s Putin.

Actual Article Body:
At the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Iran's president struck a defiant tone while Ukraine's Zelensky warned of the danger posed by Russia's Putin.

• Defiant speech: On the second day of the UN General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” Separately, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US-Iran mediated talks did not yield any major breakthrough.

• Zelensky’s warning: In his remarks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. As he spoke, Zelensky’s party headquarters were struck by Russia, according to Kyiv officials.

• All eyes on Venezuela: The country’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez addressed the UN General Assembly more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro. She said Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy — but didn’t specify when — and thanked Trump for his “readiness” toward diplomacy.

Our live coverage of the second day of the United Nations General Assembly has ended. You can catch up on Day 1 of the UNGA here.

Scroll through the posts below for more updates from today.

The second day of the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly featured more speeches from world leaders, including addresses from Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Here are some highlights:

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to attend the G20 summit in Miami, Florida in December, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday, adding “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”

If the Russian leader does accept it will be his first time attending the summit in-person since 2019, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and could provide an opportunity for a direct meeting with US President Donald Trump, who he last met in Alaska last year.

But ahead of the G20, there is another annual international forum where both Putin and Trump could also meet: the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen, China this November, hosted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The annual summit groups together 21 countries accounting for more than half of global trade, and has previously seen several landmark meetings between world leaders and high-stakes talks.

Last year, Trump skipped the summit, which took place in Gyeongju, South Korea, but he did meet China’s Xi on the sidelines in a major meeting that made progress in easing their crippling trade dispute.

Putin is expected to attend the summit in China, according to Russian state media –– his first appearance at APEC since 2017 in Vietnam, where he and Trump briefly spoke and shook hands.

A Kremlin aide recently raised the prospect of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of the world’s three major powers at APEC in November, state news agency TASS has reported. The likelihood of such a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi, is perhaps slim, but if it were to go ahead, would be unprecedented.

Trump has yet to officially confirm his attendance at APEC, but has previously hinted at a return to China this year.

Ukraine recently sent two North Korean soldiers captured fighting for Russia to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the UN General Assembly.

Zelensky shared some details of the capture, saying “One of them, when he realized he was he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. He was shocked that fate didn’t let him die. This is how they raise people in the north.”

South Korea said it could not confirm any details about the two soldiers in a statement from the foreign ministry Thursday local time, adding the issue was a “sensitive matter involving the safety and security of the individuals and their families.”
